prime.problem: The training loss only measures how well the net fits names it has already seen. A net that memorises its data gets a tiny training loss and is useless on new names, and without held-out data you can't tell the two apart, or know whether to make the model bigger or smaller.
prime.fits: The previous cards trained the MLP and read its loss on all 228,146 rows. This card splits the names first, so the same loss becomes a diagnostic. It turns the overfit-one-batch result from a sanity check into a warning, and it sets up the next card's experiment with bigger embeddings.
expect: train / dev / test splits (80/10/10 of the names)
hyperparameters: settings you choose, not learn
capacity: hidden size as a knob
prime.goal: Split the data correctly, read a pair of train/dev losses and say whether to grow the model or rein it in, and explain why the test set is opened only once.

attend: Why does the code split the 32,033 names rather than the 228,146 (context → next char) rows?
Choosing a hidden size by its dev loss is itself a kind of fitting. Fitting to what, and which pile protects you from it?
Why does a gap near zero point to a model that is too small, not to one that is just right?
Tripling the hidden layer bought only 0.03 of dev loss. What does that say about where the bottleneck is?
After only the lr 0.1 phase the 300-unit net was behind the 100-unit one. Why doesn't that mean the bigger net is worse?

must: The net only ever sees training rows → its training loss rewards memorising them → a low training loss can't tell fitting from memorising → score a held-out dev set (the 32-example net: train 0.2561, dev 13.6218)
Each setting kept because dev got lower → dev leaks into your choices → dev loss becomes slightly optimistic → keep a test set unopened and look at it once, for the honest final number

Train ≈ dev (gap −0.0009) → the net can't even fit the data it trains on → too little capacity (underfitting) → grow the model; train far below dev → memorising (overfitting) → more data, smaller model, or stop earlier
Hidden 100 → 300 (3,481 → 10,281 params) moves dev only 2.3279 → 2.2976 → the hidden layer wasn't the bottleneck → suspect another part: the 2-D embedding each character is squeezed into
elevated: The split is over names, not rows → all of a name's rows land in one pile → dev can't contain the next character of a name the net trained on, so the dev loss isn't flattered by near-duplicates

Bigger nets need more steps: after 30k steps at lr 0.1 the 300-unit net's dev was 2.4920 vs 2.3988 → compare sizes only after both have trained to a plateau, or you'll pick the smaller one for the wrong reason
reference: evaluating a split: the forward pass on all of Xdev under torch.no_grad(), then F.cross_entropy
makemore.py's own held-out set: min(1,000, 10%) of the names

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences why one loss number isn't enough and what the three piles are for. Or draw the flow names → shuffle → train / dev / test and label what each pile is allowed to change.
checklist: the training loss rewards memorising, so you need names the net never trained on
train fits the parameters; dev compares hyperparameters; test is looked at once at the end
choosing by dev leaks dev into your choices, which is why test exists
gap ≈ 0 → underfitting → grow the model; big gap → overfitting → more data, smaller model, stop earlier
split names after a shuffle, not rows

retrieve.q: Explain why the 32-example net's loss of 0.2561 was a good sign on the overfit card and a bad sign here, using its dev loss.
answer: on the overfit card it only checked that the training loop works
on dev names it scores 13.6218, far worse than a uniform guess (3.2958)
a low loss on seen data measures memorising, not generalising

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to one name, say emma, from random.shuffle(words) to a dev loss. Where do its 5 rows end up, and at which step could it influence the parameters?
answer: the shuffle puts the name at some position; its slice (train, dev or test) is set by n1 and n2
build_dataset turns it into 5 rows, all in that same split
only if it landed in train can a minibatch pick its rows and move the parameters
in dev it only contributes to the averaged cross-entropy that you read

retrieve.q: Your net ends at train 2.13 / dev 2.17 and you have one more experiment. Do you grow the hidden layer or add more data? What does each cost, and what would tell you that you chose wrong?
answer: a gap of 0.04 is opening, so it has started to overfit a little: more data (or regularisation) attacks that, and growing the net may widen it
a bigger net costs compute and steps; more data costs collecting it
wrong choice shows up as dev not improving while train keeps falling

retrieve.q: Why is it a mistake to report the dev loss of your best configuration as your model's final quality?
answer: you picked the configuration because its dev loss was lowest, so that number is biased low
a fresh test set, touched once, gives the unbiased estimate

compare.q: Both cards drive the training loss down on data the net sees. What is fundamentally different about what each loss is used for, and when is a very low training loss what you want?
answer: overfit-one-batch: low loss on 32 rows proves the loop and the gradients work
here: training loss is compared with dev to diagnose capacity
you want it very low only as a debugging check; for a real model you want low dev loss, and train alone never shows that

compare.q: The learning-rate sweep and the hidden-size experiment both choose a hyperparameter. Which loss should each be judged on, and how does choosing on the wrong one fail?
answer: the lr sweep watches training minibatch losses, because it asks how fast the net learns
hidden size (capacity) must be judged on dev, because a bigger net can lower train by memorising
choosing capacity on train always favours the biggest net, and overfits

compare.q: This card grows the hidden layer and barely moves dev; the next grows the embedding and moves it more. Which design choice makes the embedding the tighter bottleneck, and what would the gap look like if you overshot?
answer: every character has to pass through 2 numbers before the hidden layer sees it, so extra hidden units can't recover what the embedding throws away
10-D embeddings widen that path
overshooting shows up as train dropping while dev stalls, as in the final 2.1260 / 2.1701

predict.q: Keep the 300-unit net and the same 50,000-step schedule, but train it on only the first 1,000 shuffled training names (7,170 rows) instead of 25,626. Predict the final train and dev losses: which one moves, and in which direction?
predict.answer: Train falls to 1.9988, below anything the full-data runs reached, while dev rises to 2.5452. The gap jumps from about 0 to 0.5464: the same net that underfit 182,625 rows overfits 7,170. Over- or underfitting depends on the model and the amount of data together, not on the model alone.

apply.task: Copy labs/splits-and-fit.py to your own file. Build a small training set from the first 1,000 names of the seed-42 shuffle (build_dataset(ws[:1000])), train the 300-unit net on it with the same two phases (30,000 steps at lr 0.1, then 20,000 at 0.01), and print train and dev after each phase. Then write one sentence for each phase naming the diagnosis and the fix.
apply.done: You see 7,170 training rows, train 2.2140 / dev 2.7112 after the first phase and train 1.9988 / dev 2.5452 after the second, and your diagnosis says overfitting (gap 0.5464) with more data as the fix.
apply.hint: Shuffle a copy: ws = list(words); random.seed(42); random.shuffle(ws). Score train on the small set itself, and dev on the usual Xdev.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how little the 300-unit net helped, or how far dev rose on 1,000 names?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why a gap near zero means too small, or why picking on dev makes dev optimistic?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: gap size → diagnosis, or diagnosis → which fix to try?
Where in your own past projects did you report a number that you had also tuned on?
What will you watch for when the next card grows the embedding to 10 dimensions?
